options: The exterior paint dry-film thickness at one point on the shell
Shell-bottom elevations at intervals around the tank circumference
The product temperature at the center of the stored liquid
The torque on the bolts of the lowest nozzle flange joint
content.explanation: Settlement surveys record elevations at stations around the perimeter, then compare them to a reference (often a best-fit curve).

content.stem: API 653 generally requires a hydrostatic test after which of the following?
options: Major alterations or reconstruction affecting the tank's integrity
Any routine external visual inspection of the tank in service
Repainting the exterior shell with a new protective coating
Replacing a single gauge on the fixed roof of the tank
content.explanation: A hydrotest is required after reconstruction or major alterations/repairs affecting integrity, unless waived by an engineer per the standard.

content.stem: The purpose of the API 653 hydrostatic test is to:
options: Establish the cathodic protection potential of the tank floor underside
Confirm the tank's structural integrity and leak-tightness under load
Set the joint efficiency value used in the shell-thickness design formula
Measure the exterior protective shell paint thickness over the seams
content.explanation: The hydrotest loads the tank with water to verify integrity and reveal leaks before return to service.

content.stem: When hydrotesting a tank, control of the test-water temperature matters because:
options: Cold water improves the exterior paint adhesion on the shell
Warmer water always increases the measured shell thickness reading
Low metal temperature with the test load raises brittle-fracture risk
Water temperature sets the maximum permitted fill height directly
content.explanation: A full hydrotest at low metal temperature combines high stress with reduced toughness, so brittle-fracture risk is assessed before testing.

content.stem: API 653 brittle-fracture screening of an existing tank primarily compares:
options: Exterior shell paint gloss against the surrounding tank coating colors used
Material toughness against thickness, stress, and minimum metal temperature
Roof vent count against the number of nozzles fitted in the lower shell course
Welder qualification dates against the original tank construction records
content.explanation: Brittle-fracture assessment screens toughness versus thickness, stress level, and the lowest expected metal temperature, often via an exemption curve.

content.stem: The brittle-fracture exemption curve in API 653 is used for carbon steel of:
options: Any material, to set the cathodic protection criterion for the floor
Known high toughness only, where no assessment is ever needed
Unknown toughness, to screen acceptable thickness versus temperature
Stainless construction, to choose the exterior coating system
content.explanation: The exemption curve screens carbon steel of unknown toughness, relating allowable thickness to the minimum metal temperature for continued service.

content.stem: A tank that has operated for years at its current conditions without brittle fracture is generally considered to have:
options: An automatically increased maximum allowable fill height granted right now
No need for inspection of any kind at all for the remainder of its life
A permanently exempt status regardless of any future colder service later
Demonstrated fitness for those conditions, pending any change in service
content.explanation: Prior successful service at the same conditions is evidence of fitness, but lowering temperature or raising stress triggers a new evaluation.

content.stem: RP 575 inspection of a tank foundation looks for:
options: Settlement, erosion, and deterioration of the supporting ringwall or pad
The exterior shell paint color match to the adjacent rows of storage tanks
The torque that was applied to the topmost shell course weld seams
The number of product samples that were drawn during the last work shift
content.explanation: Foundation inspection checks for settlement, washout/erosion, cracking of ringwalls, and drainage that could undermine support.

content.stem: Proper drainage around a tank foundation is emphasized because standing water can:
options: Improve the exterior paint adhesion on the lower shell course
Increase the joint efficiency of the lower shell course
Raise the brittle-fracture exemption temperature of the steel
Promote underside corrosion and contribute to edge settlement
content.explanation: Water trapped under the tank drives soil-side corrosion and can soften support, contributing to edge settlement.

content.stem: Two common ways to mitigate soil-side corrosion of a tank bottom are:
options: Cathodic protection of the underside and an under-tank liner or coating
Raising the product specific gravity and adding more roof vents
Repainting the exterior shell and replacing the level gauge unit
Increasing the joint efficiency and lowering the maximum fill height
content.explanation: Soil-side bottom corrosion is mitigated by cathodic protection (per RP 651) and/or barriers such as under-tank liners and coatings.

content.stem: When evaluating an existing tank whose original radiography records are unavailable, the inspector selecting joint efficiency E should:
options: Ignore E entirely and use only the nominal plate thickness value instead
Always assume full radiography and a value of one for all of the seams
Use the efficiency justified by the known or assumed examination level
Set E from the exterior shell paint thickness measured over the weld seam
content.explanation: Without records, E is taken consistent with the examination that can be justified for the original construction; an unjustified high E is non-conservative.

content.stem: API 653 specifies minimum dimensions for a bottom replacement plate primarily to:
options: Keep new weld seams away from existing welds and ensure sound joints
Match the exterior protective shell paint color to the adjacent plates
Increase the maximum fill height that is allowed for the storage tank
Reduce the number of fixed-roof vents that are required on the tank roof
content.explanation: Minimum replacement-plate sizes keep new welds spaced from existing seams and avoid stress concentrations, ensuring sound repairs.

content.stem: API 653 allows extending the internal inspection interval beyond the usual ceiling when:
options: The tank has more roof vents than the original design required
The exterior shell has simply been repainted a brighter color
The operator prefers a longer interval for scheduling reasons
A risk-based inspection assessment supports the longer interval
content.explanation: RBI per API 653 can justify intervals beyond the default ceiling, based on probability and consequence of failure with documented analysis.

content.stem: Before placing a tank into a more severe service than its history, API 653 expects the owner to:
options: Simply repaint the exterior shell to the new product color code scheme
Evaluate suitability for the new service, including thinning and toughness
Raise the maximum fill height to match the denser new product stored
Remove the cathodic protection system entirely from the tank bottom
content.explanation: A change to more severe service (denser product, lower temperature, corrosivity) triggers a suitability evaluation covering thickness, toughness, and corrosion.

content.stem: Installing a new bottom over an existing one (a double bottom) is used to:
options: Replace the need for any future internal inspection of the tank
Increase the tank's maximum allowable fill height directly
Restore bottom integrity while providing a leak-detection space
Eliminate the requirement for cathodic protection permanently
content.explanation: A double bottom restores integrity and can create an interstitial space for leak detection, subject to API 653 repair requirements.

content.stem: API 650 1-foot method, bottom course: D = 100 ft, H = 48 ft, G = 1.0, Sd = 25300 psi, E = 0.85, CA = 0.0625 in. Design shell thickness td = 2.6 D (H-1) G/(Sd E) + CA?
content.explanation: td = (2.6 x 100 x (48-1) x 1.0)/(25300 x 0.85) + 0.0625 = 0.568 + 0.0625 = 0.6307 in. The design condition uses G and adds the corrosion allowance.

content.stem: Same tank (D = 100 ft, H = 48 ft, E = 0.85) with a test allowable St = 28500 psi. Hydrostatic test thickness tt = 2.6 D (H-1)/(St E)?
content.explanation: tt = (2.6 x 100 x (48-1))/(28500 x 0.85) = 0.5044 in. The test condition uses no specific gravity (water) and adds no corrosion allowance.

content.stem: For the bottom course above, td = 0.631 in (design) and tt = 0.504 in (test). The required shell thickness is the greater of the two, which is:
content.explanation: Required thickness = greater of td and tt = max(0.631, 0.504) = 0.631 in; here the design condition governs.

content.stem: API 650 1-foot method: D = 80 ft, H = 40 ft, G = 0.9, Sd = 20000 psi, E = 0.85, CA = 0.0625 in. Design shell thickness td?
For that tank (D = 80 ft, H = 40 ft, E = 0.85), the test allowable is St = 24900 psi. Hydrostatic test thickness tt?
API 650 1-foot method for an upper course: D = 100 ft, H = 16 ft (bottom of that course to top liquid), G = 1.0, Sd = 25300 psi, E = 0.85, CA = 0.0625 in. Design thickness td?
content.explanation: td = (2.6 x 100 x (16-1) x 1.0)/(25300 x 0.85) + 0.0625 = 0.1814 + 0.0625 = 0.2439 in. H is measured from the bottom of the course being designed.

content.stem: For that upper course (D = 100 ft, H = 16 ft, E = 0.85, St = 28500 psi), the hydrostatic test thickness tt is:
API 650 sets a minimum nominal shell-plate thickness that increases with tank diameter because:
options: Larger tanks always store a denser product than smaller ones do
Larger-diameter shells need more thickness for handling and stability
The exterior paint must be thicker on a larger storage tank shell
A wider tank has a brighter identification color requirement set
content.explanation: Minimum shell thickness rises with diameter (e.g., 3/16 in for small tanks up to 5/16 in or more for large ones) for handling, welding, and stability, independent of the stress calc.

content.stem: The API 650 1-foot method is permitted for shell design when the tank diameter is:
options: Within the limit (200 ft or less) where the simpler method applies
Greater than 200 ft, where only the 1-foot method is allowed
Any size at all, since the method has no diameter limitation
Below the minimum size that requires any shell calculation
content.explanation: The 1-foot method applies to tanks up to 200 ft diameter; larger tanks use the more economical variable-design-point method.

content.stem: Compared with the 1-foot method, the variable-design-point method generally yields:
options: Thicker courses everywhere, with no possible material savings
Thinner upper courses, saving material on large-diameter tanks
Identical thicknesses, making the method choice irrelevant always
A result independent of the tank diameter or course height
content.explanation: The VDP method accounts for the restraint at the course boundaries and typically permits thinner upper courses than the conservative 1-foot method.

content.stem: API 650 requires butt-welded annular plates (rather than a lap-welded bottom) when:
options: The exterior shell paint color must match the adjacent storage tank
The hydrostatic stress in the first shell course is high enough to require them
The tank has fewer roof vents than the original design called for
The product specific gravity stored in the tank is below one
content.explanation: Butt-welded annular plates are required when the first-course stress (and shell thickness) exceed thresholds, giving a stronger shell-to-bottom region.

content.stem: A self-supporting cone roof differs from a column-supported cone roof in that it:
options: Is used only on open-top tanks with no fixed roof at all
Always floats directly on the surface of the stored product
Requires no connection at all to the top of the tank shell
Carries roof loads through the shell without internal support columns
content.explanation: A self-supporting roof transfers loads to the shell with no internal columns; a supported roof uses rafters and columns.

content.stem: A frangible (weak) roof-to-shell joint is designed so that, on overpressure, the:
options: Shell-to-bottom joint fails first to relieve the pressure safely
Roof-to-shell joint fails before the shell-to-bottom joint does
Tank bottom lifts uniformly off the foundation ringwall pad
Exterior shell paint blisters to vent the excess vapor pressure
content.explanation: A frangible joint is the intended weak point: it lets the roof separate (venting up) before the shell-to-bottom joint fails, keeping product contained.

content.stem: An external floating roof differs from an internal floating roof primarily in that the external type:
options: Cannot be used on any petroleum storage service at all
Always stores a denser product than the internal type
Is exposed to weather with no fixed roof above it
Provides the cathodic protection for the tank floor plates
content.explanation: An external floating roof is open to weather (needs drainage and seals for rain/wind); an internal floating roof sits under a fixed roof.

content.stem: An intermediate wind girder may be added to a tall open-top tank when:
options: The tank stores a product with a specific gravity below one
The exterior paint color needs to be changed on the upper shell
The shell is too tall to remain stable against wind without it
The number of roof vents exceeds the original design quantity
content.explanation: Intermediate wind girders are added when the unstiffened shell height exceeds the limit for wind stability, supplementing the top wind girder.

content.stem: Reinforcement around a shell nozzle in API 650 is provided to:
options: Lower the brittle-fracture exemption temperature of the shell
Increase the joint efficiency of the adjacent shell course welds
Replace the shell cross-sectional area removed by the opening
Provide the exterior coating anchor around the nozzle neck
content.explanation: Reinforcement replaces the load-carrying area lost at the opening, keeping stresses around the penetration acceptable (area-replacement basis).

content.stem: Seismic design of a storage tank (API 650 Annex E) evaluates, among other things, the:
options: Overturning stability and sloshing of the liquid contents
Exterior shell paint adhesion under ground acceleration
Joint efficiency increase available during an earthquake
Number of roof vents required for thermal venting only
content.explanation: Seismic design addresses overturning, shell compression, anchorage, and liquid sloshing (freeboard) under ground motion.

content.stem: Tank shell anchorage is provided primarily to resist:
options: Uplift from wind, seismic, or internal pressure loads
The hydrostatic head of the stored product alone
The exterior corrosion of the lower shell course
The thermal expansion of the fixed roof plates only
content.explanation: Anchors resist net uplift from wind overturning, seismic, or internal pressure that would otherwise lift the shell off the foundation.

content.stem: API 650 assigns plate materials to toughness groups (e.g., via the design-metal-temperature curves) in order to:
options: Fix the maximum number of nozzles allowed in each shell course
Set the exterior paint color code for each material group used
Determine the cathodic protection current for the tank floor
Ensure adequate notch toughness at the lowest expected service temperature
content.explanation: Material group/toughness selection ensures the steel has adequate notch toughness at the design metal temperature, guarding against brittle fracture.

content.stem: API 650 sets a levelness tolerance on the tank foundation because an out-of-level base can:
options: Induce shell distortion and uneven loading during filling
Improve the exterior paint adhesion on the lower shell
Raise the maximum allowable fill height of the tank
Eliminate the need for any settlement survey afterward
content.explanation: Foundation levelness limits (e.g., a small tolerance per length of circumference) prevent shell distortion and peaking/banding stresses.

content.stem: In the API 650 design-thickness equation, the corrosion allowance is:
options: Added equally to both the design and the test thicknesses
Subtracted from the calculated design thickness before use
Added to the calculated design thickness, not the test thickness
Ignored entirely because tanks do not corrode in service
content.explanation: CA is added to the design thickness td; the hydrostatic test thickness tt does not include CA (the tank is tested in the as-built, uncorroded state).

content.stem: Welding procedures and welders for tank repair work are qualified in accordance with:
options: The cathodic protection criteria for the tank floor
The exterior shell paint specification for the tank
ASME Section IX, as referenced by API 653 and API 650
The product specific gravity stored within the tank
content.explanation: API 653/650 reference ASME Section IX for qualifying welding procedures (WPS/PQR) and welders (WPQ).

content.stem: Vertical and horizontal joints in an API 650 tank shell are:
options: Riveted joints in all modern welded steel storage tanks
Always lap-welded joints regardless of the shell course
Left unwelded and sealed only with an exterior coating
Butt-welded joints with full penetration for the shell plates
content.explanation: Shell vertical and horizontal seams are full-penetration butt welds; lap joints are used on the bottom, not the shell.

content.stem: Tank bottom plates (away from the annular region) are commonly joined by:
options: Threaded connections between adjacent bottom plate sections
Full-penetration butt welds required across the entire bottom
An adhesive bond with no welding of the bottom plates at all
Lap welds with a single fillet on the top side of the plates
content.explanation: Interior bottom plates are typically lap-welded (single fillet top side); the annular region near the shell may require butt welds.

content.stem: Preheat may be applied before welding on a tank to:
options: Increase the exterior paint adhesion over the finished weld
Reduce cooling rate and the risk of cracking in the weld zone
Raise the joint efficiency used in the shell-design formula
Lower the cathodic protection potential required for the floor
content.explanation: Preheat slows cooling, lowering hardness and hydrogen-cracking risk in susceptible steels and thicker sections.

content.stem: Welding on a tank that remains in service requires special attention to:
options: Burn-through risk and the flammability of the contained product
Matching the exterior shell paint color to the adjacent tanks
Increasing the maximum fill height during the welding work
Reducing the number of roof vents on the fixed tank roof
content.explanation: In-service welding must manage burn-through (remaining wall, heat input) and the fire/explosion hazard of the product and vapors.

content.stem: Radiographic examination of new tank shell butt welds is used to detect:
options: The cathodic protection potential at the shell-to-bottom joint
The exterior paint thickness applied over the finished weld
The welder break schedule recorded during the shift work
Buried volumetric flaws such as porosity, slag, and lack of fusion
content.explanation: RT images buried (volumetric) discontinuities in the butt welds; its extent on shell joints is set by API 650/653 requirements.

content.stem: The required extent of radiography on tank shell welds depends primarily on the:
options: Shell thickness and the joint type, per the API 650/653 rules
Exterior shell paint color selected for the storage tank
Number of nozzles installed in the lowest shell course
Product specific gravity that the tank is designed to store
content.explanation: RT extent (spot locations and number) scales with shell thickness and joint category per the API 650 radiography requirements that API 653 invokes.

content.stem: A vacuum-box test on a tank bottom weld is used to find:
options: Buried slag deep within the thickness of the bottom plate
Through-leaks in the weld by drawing bubbles from a soap film
The remaining thickness of the annular plate near the shell
The cathodic protection current reaching the bottom plate
content.explanation: A vacuum box over a soap-filmed weld reveals through-leaks as bubbles; it tests tightness, not buried-flaw depth.

content.stem: Magnetic particle or liquid penetrant examination of a tank repair weld is used to detect:
options: The product specific gravity inside the storage tank
Buried volumetric porosity deep within the weld metal
The exterior paint adhesion over the completed weld
Surface-breaking cracks and discontinuities in the weld
content.explanation: MT and PT find surface-breaking flaws; MT suits ferromagnetic steel, PT any nonporous surface. RT/UT are used for buried flaws.

content.stem: After reconstructing a tank, the new and re-welded joints are examined because reconstruction:
options: Removes the need for any hydrostatic test of the rebuilt tank
Always lowers the joint efficiency to zero for the rebuilt shell
Introduces new welds whose quality must be verified before service
Raises the brittle-fracture exemption temperature automatically
content.explanation: Reconstruction creates new welds that receive NDE (and usually a hydrotest) to confirm integrity before the tank returns to service.

content.stem: A change to an essential variable on a welding procedure in Section IX requires:
options: Only a change to the exterior shell paint color code
Requalification of the welding procedure specification
No action at all because essential variables are optional
A reduction in the tank's maximum allowable fill height
content.explanation: Changing an essential variable (e.g., process, base/filler grouping, key parameters) requires the WPS to be requalified by a new PQR.

content.stem: A welder performance qualification (WPQ) in Section IX establishes that the welder can:
options: Set the cathodic protection criterion for the tank bottom
Select the exterior shell paint system for the storage tank
Deposit sound weld metal within the qualified range of variables
Determine the maximum fill height permitted for the tank
content.explanation: The WPQ demonstrates the welder's ability to produce sound welds within the qualified positions and ranges; it is distinct from the WPS/PQR.

content.stem: To evaluate a suspected crack at a tank shell-to-bottom weld, the most appropriate NDE is:
options: A surface method such as magnetic particle examination
Cathodic protection potential measurement of the floor
Exterior shell paint thickness measurement at the weld
A vacuum-box test, which only finds through-leaks not cracks
content.explanation: A suspected surface-breaking crack is best found with a surface method such as magnetic particle examination; the other choices either reveal only through-leaks or are unrelated to crack detection.

content.stem: In the shell-thickness formulas, the design liquid level H for a course is measured from the:
options: Nearest nozzle centerline to the top angle of the tank shell
Top of the tank shell down to the bottom of the lowest course
Center of the tank bottom to the top of the fixed roof plates
Bottom of the course under consideration to the maximum liquid level
content.explanation: H is taken from the bottom of the course being designed up to the maximum design liquid level (or overflow), so lower courses see the greatest H.

content.stem: API 653 external inspection interval is the lesser of 5 years or RCA/(4N), where RCA = measured - required thickness and N is the shell corrosion rate. Measured shell = 0.360 in, required = 0.300 in, N = 0.005 in/yr. The external interval is:
options: 5 years
6 years
3 years
12 years

content.stem: Using the lesser of 5 years or RCA/(4N): measured shell = 0.500 in, required = 0.300 in, N = 0.004 in/yr. The external inspection interval is:
options: 10 years
12.5 years
25 years
5 years
content.explanation: RCA = 0.200. RCA/(4N) = 0.200/0.016 = 12.5 yr, but the 5-year ceiling governs, so 5 years.

content.stem: The API 653 shell ultrasonic-thickness interval is the lesser of 15 years or RCA/(2N). Measured shell = 0.420 in, required = 0.300 in, N = 0.006 in/yr. The UT interval is:
options: 10 years
15 years
5 years
20 years
content.explanation: RCA = 0.120. RCA/(2N) = 0.120/(2 x 0.006) = 10.0; the lesser of 15 and 10 is 10 years.

content.stem: Using the lesser of 15 years or RCA/(2N): measured shell = 0.500 in, required = 0.280 in, N = 0.005 in/yr. The shell UT interval is:
options: 22 years
15 years
11 years
5 years
content.explanation: RCA = 0.220. RCA/(2N) = 0.220/0.010 = 22 yr, but the 15-year ceiling governs, so 15 years.

content.stem: A tank bottom's deepest soil-side pit is 0.150 in after 12 years of service. The maximum bottom corrosion rate used for the evaluation is:
options: 0.025 in/yr
content.explanation: The maximum rate uses the deepest penetration over the period: 0.150/12 = 0.0125 in/yr.

content.stem: A tank bottom's minimum remaining thickness is 0.220 in, the required MRT is 0.100 in, and the maximum corrosion rate is 0.0125 in/yr. Remaining life of the bottom?
options: 17.6 years
9.6 years
4.8 years
8 years
content.explanation: Remaining life = (t_actual - MRT)/rate = (0.220 - 0.100)/0.0125 = 9.6 years.

content.stem: API 653 defines the critical zone of the tank bottom as the portion within:
options: 3 in. of the inside edge of the shell, measured radially inward
12 in. of the exact center point of the tank bottom plates
1 in. of every interior lap weld across the entire bottom
6 in. of the nearest roof support column base plate inside
content.explanation: The critical zone is the bottom/annular region within 3 in. of the inside of the shell, where shell-to-bottom stresses concentrate.

content.stem: When inspecting an external floating roof, RP 575 gives particular attention to the:
options: Welder qualification records for the original shell seams
Exterior shell paint color match to the neighboring tanks
Cathodic protection potential of the tank bottom plates
Pontoon integrity, drains, and the perimeter seal condition
content.explanation: Floating-roof inspection covers pontoon/deck integrity, roof drains, and seals, since failures there cause sinking or vapor loss.

content.stem: RP 575 includes tank appurtenances such as nozzles, manways, and gauging devices in the inspection because they:
options: Set the cathodic protection criterion for the tank bottom plate
Determine the joint efficiency used in the shell-design formula
Are potential leak and corrosion sites that affect tank integrity
Establish the maximum allowable fill height for the storage tank
content.explanation: Appurtenances (nozzles, manways, gauges, vents) are inspected as potential leak paths and corrosion/mechanical-damage sites.

content.stem: Before an internal inspection, RP 575 emphasizes cleaning and gas-freeing the tank chiefly to:
options: Raise the cathodic protection potential of the floor plates
Increase the joint efficiency of the lower shell course welds
Provide safe entry and expose the surfaces for examination
Match the exterior shell paint to the adjacent storage tanks
content.explanation: Cleaning and gas-freeing make entry safe and expose floor/shell surfaces so corrosion and defects can actually be found.

content.stem: RP 575 notes that ultrasonic thickness readings on a tank shell are used to:
options: Detect surface-breaking cracks at the shell-to-bottom weld
Quantify remaining wall and support corrosion-rate calculations
Measure the exterior protective paint film thickness applied
Establish the cathodic protection current for the floor plate
content.explanation: UT gauging quantifies remaining shell thickness, feeding corrosion-rate and remaining-life evaluation; surface cracks need MT/PT.

content.stem: On an insulated tank, RP 575 highlights the risk of corrosion under insulation (CUI) where:
options: Moisture is trapped against the shell beneath damaged insulation
The product specific gravity stored in the tank is below one
The tank has more roof vents than the original design called for
The exterior paint color does not match the adjacent tanks
content.explanation: CUI develops where water penetrates and is held against the shell under insulation, especially in the wet/dry temperature range.

content.stem: RP 575 indicates the inspection frequency for a tank should be based primarily on its:
options: Brand of level gauge fitted to the tank fixed roof nozzle
Exterior shell paint color and the gloss of the coating
Number of roof support columns inside the storage tank
Service history, corrosion rates, and consequence of failure
content.explanation: Frequency is risk-driven: service history, measured corrosion, and consequence guide how often and how thoroughly a tank is inspected.

content.stem: A commonly applied cathodic-protection criterion in RP 651 for a steel tank bottom is a:
options: Polarized potential of -850 mV relative to a copper/copper-sulfate reference
Fixed exterior paint thickness of 0.85 mils over the tank shell
Joint efficiency of 0.85 on the lower shell course welds
Specific gravity of 0.85 for the product stored in the tank
content.explanation: CP adequacy is judged against potential criteria such as -850 mV (polarized) versus a Cu/CuSO4 reference electrode.

content.stem: RP 651 treats low soil resistivity beneath a tank as significant because it:
options: Raises the brittle-fracture exemption temperature of steel
Improves the exterior paint adhesion on the lower shell
Increases corrosion current and the soil-side corrosion risk
Reduces the hydrostatic head acting on the bottom plates
content.explanation: Lower soil resistivity allows more corrosion current to flow, raising soil-side corrosion risk and influencing CP design.

content.stem: A structure-to-soil potential survey under RP 651 is performed to:
options: Determine the maximum fill height permitted for the tank
Measure the exterior shell paint thickness around the chime
Set the joint efficiency for the reconstructed tank shell
Verify the tank bottom is adequately polarized by the CP system
content.explanation: Structure-to-soil potential measurements confirm the floor is polarized to the protective criterion across the CP system.

content.stem: A galvanic (sacrificial-anode) CP system is generally preferred over impressed current when:
options: The current demand is low and a simple, self-powered system suffices
The tank stores a product with a specific gravity above one
The exterior shell requires a brighter protective paint color
The number of roof vents exceeds the original design quantity
content.explanation: Galvanic systems suit low current demand and need no external power; impressed-current systems suit higher demand or high-resistivity soils.

content.stem: RP 651 calls for cathodic-protection effectiveness records to be retained for:
options: No time at all, since CP data has no inspection value
A defined period (such as five years) to demonstrate continued protection
Only the single day the survey readings were taken
The exterior paint warranty period of the tank shell only
content.explanation: CP effectiveness records are kept for a defined period (e.g., five years) to show ongoing protection and support trending.

content.stem: RP 652 distinguishes thin-film from thick-film reinforced linings primarily by:
options: Film thickness and whether reinforcement is incorporated into the lining
The exterior shell paint color applied above the chime angle
The joint efficiency of the lower shell course weld seams
The specific gravity of the product the tank is storing
content.explanation: Thin-film linings are thinner and unreinforced; thick-film linings are heavier and often reinforced, with different durability and cost.

content.stem: RP 652 notes that inorganic-zinc (zinc-silicate) coatings applied at a few mils DFT are:
options: Always treated as the thickest reinforced lining available for tanks
Not counted as thin-film linings for API 653 thickness-calculation purposes
A substitute for cathodic protection of the soil-side bottom
A means of raising the joint efficiency of the shell welds
content.explanation: Inorganic-zinc coatings at ~3-5 mils are not credited as thin-film linings in API 653 bottom calculations, though they offer some protection.

content.stem: RP 652 specifies abrasive blasting to a defined profile before lining because:
options: It raises the maximum fill height permitted for the storage tank
It establishes the cathodic protection potential of the floor
Adhesion and lining life depend on cleanliness and surface profile
It sets the joint efficiency used in the shell-design formula
content.explanation: A clean, properly profiled substrate is essential for lining adhesion; inadequate prep is a leading cause of early lining failure.

content.stem: A holiday test on a newly applied tank-bottom lining is used to find:
options: Buried slag within the bottom plate base metal
Pinholes and discontinuities in the lining film
The remaining thickness of the annular plate ring
The cathodic protection current reaching the floor
content.explanation: Holiday (spark) testing detects pinholes and bare spots in the lining that would let product reach the steel.

content.stem: Selecting a tank-bottom lining under RP 652 depends most on the:
options: Joint efficiency used in the shell-thickness calculation
Exterior shell paint color chosen for the storage tank
Number of nozzles installed in the lowest shell course
Stored product and service conditions the lining must resist
content.explanation: Lining choice is driven by chemical compatibility with the stored product and the service (temperature, immersion) it must withstand.

content.stem: Atmospheric corrosion on the exterior of a storage tank shell is most aggressive:
options: Where moisture collects and dwells, such as at the chime and supports
On the warmest, driest, and best-ventilated upper shell course
Only on the interior wetted surface of the lowest shell course
Where the exterior paint is thickest and least likely to fail
content.explanation: Atmospheric corrosion concentrates where moisture lingers (chime, supports, crevices, marine/humid exposure), not on dry, well-drained surfaces.

content.stem: Corrosion under insulation on a storage tank is of greatest concern in the temperature range where:
options: The exterior protective paint is at its maximum design thickness
The steel is always far above the boiling point of any water
The product specific gravity stored in the tank is below one
Water can be present and cyclically wet and dry the steel surface
content.explanation: CUI is worst where temperatures allow water to persist and cycle wet/dry; very hot or very cold surfaces that stay dry are less affected.

content.stem: Brittle fracture of a tank shell is most likely when:
options: The tank operates warm with low stress and tough material
Low metal temperature combines with high stress and low toughness
The exterior paint color is darker than the adjacent tanks
The product specific gravity is exactly equal to one point zero
content.explanation: Brittle fracture needs the combination of low temperature, a flaw/high stress, and low toughness; warm tough steel at modest stress resists it.

content.stem: Caustic corrosion in a tank storing caustic solution is accelerated by:
options: A lower product specific gravity in the stored solution only
The exterior shell paint color applied above the chime line
Concentration of caustic and elevated temperature at the surface
The number of roof vents fitted on the fixed tank roof
content.explanation: Caustic corrosion accelerates with caustic concentration and temperature; localized concentration (e.g., at heat-transfer or splash zones) worsens it.

content.stem: A non-stress-relieved carbon-steel tank in concentrated caustic service cracks at welds. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Atmospheric corrosion of the shell
Caustic stress corrosion cracking
Soil-side corrosion of the floor
Sulfuric acid corrosion at velocity
content.explanation: Cracking at non-PWHT welds in concentrated caustic is caustic SCC (caustic embrittlement), driven by caustic concentration, temperature, and residual stress.

content.stem: An uninsulated tank shell in a humid coastal site shows general external rusting and scaling worst near the base. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Ethanol stress corrosion cracking
Caustic stress corrosion cracking
Atmospheric corrosion
Concentration cell corrosion under deposits
content.explanation: General external rusting in a humid/marine atmosphere, worst where moisture lingers near the base, is atmospheric corrosion.

content.stem: An insulated tank shell develops localized external wall loss beneath wet, damaged insulation in the moderate-temperature range. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Caustic corrosion at the surface
Brittle fracture of the shell plate
Soil-side corrosion of the floor
Corrosion under insulation
content.explanation: Localized external loss under wet insulation in the water-present temperature band is CUI; keeping insulation/jacketing dry mitigates it.

content.stem: A welded tank shell qualifies for a joint efficiency E = 0.85 with the required spot radiography. With D = 110 ft, H = 44 ft, G = 1.0, S = 23200 psi, the API 653 minimum thickness t = 2.6 D (H-1) G/(S E) is:
content.explanation: With spot radiography E = 0.85: t = (2.6 x 110 x 43 x 1.0)/(23200 x 0.85) = 0.6236 in. Using E = 1.0 (unjustified) understates the required thickness.

content.stem: Evaluating a reconstructed tank with the API 650 method: D = 120 ft, H = 40 ft, G = 0.95, Sd = 23200 psi, E = 0.85, CA = 0.0625 in. Design thickness td = 2.6 D (H-1) G/(Sd E) + CA?
For that reconstructed tank (D = 120 ft, H = 40 ft, E = 0.85) the test allowable is St = 24900 psi. Hydrostatic test thickness tt = 2.6 D (H-1)/(St E)?
content.explanation: tt = (2.6 x 120 x 39)/(24900 x 0.85) = 0.5749 in; the test thickness uses no specific gravity and adds no corrosion allowance.

content.stem: A riveted tank shell is assigned a joint efficiency E = 0.85 from API 653 Table 4.3 for its joint configuration. With D = 80 ft, H = 30 ft, G = 1.0, S = 21000 psi, the minimum thickness t = 2.6 D (H-1) G/(S E) is:
A shell course read 0.520 in twelve years ago and 0.412 in today. Long-term corrosion rate?
options: 0.018 in/yr
0.009 in/yr
content.explanation: Rate = (t_initial - t_actual)/time = (0.520 - 0.412)/12 = 0.009 in/yr.

content.stem: Shell course: t_actual = 0.412 in, t_min = 0.250 in, corrosion rate = 0.009 in/yr. Remaining life?
options: 9 years
45.8 years
18 years
27.8 years
content.explanation: Remaining life = (t_actual - t_min)/rate = (0.412 - 0.250)/0.009 = 18 years.

content.stem: The joint efficiency E used in the tank shell-thickness formula is determined by the:
options: Exterior protective shell paint color selected for the storage tank itself
Type of joint and the extent of radiography that can be justified
Number of nozzles that are installed in the lowest shell course of the tank
Specific gravity of the product that the tank happens to be storing now
content.explanation: E reflects the weld joint type and the radiography performed/justifiable; more examination supports a higher E.

content.stem: If the original radiography of an existing tank cannot be documented, the inspector should choose an E that is:
options: Taken from the exterior protective shell paint specification of the tank
Always taken as 1.0, since older tanks were all fully radiographed by default
Justified by the examination that can be substantiated, not assumed high
Set to exactly zero so the tank is automatically retired from all service
content.explanation: Without records, E is taken consistent with what can be justified; assuming a high E is non-conservative and overstates capacity.

content.stem: For a fixed service, lowering the joint efficiency E in the tmin formula:
options: Increases the required minimum shell thickness
Decreases the required minimum shell thickness
Has no effect on the required shell thickness
Changes only the exterior paint thickness needed
content.explanation: E is in the denominator of the tmin relation, so a lower E raises the required thickness for the same loads.

content.stem: API 653 assigns a riveted-shell joint efficiency that depends on the:
options: Number of roof support columns inside the riveted tank
Exterior shell paint color applied over the riveted seam
Product specific gravity stored within the riveted tank
Riveted joint type and configuration, taken from API 653 Table 4.3
content.explanation: Riveted joint efficiency is read from Table 4.3 by joint type/configuration (e.g., butt straps on both sides at about 0.85); 4.3.4 applies the 4.3.3.1 equation with these E values.

content.stem: Evaluating a riveted tank shell for continued service uses:
options: A separate riveted-tank minimum-thickness procedure in API 653
The same butt-weld minimum-thickness formula with no change for the rivets
Only the exterior protective paint condition observed over the riveted seams
The cathodic protection potential measured across the riveted tank shell
content.explanation: API 653 4.3.4 gives the riveted-tank evaluation, accounting for the riveted joint rather than a welded butt joint.

content.stem: API 653 generally prohibits hot taps on a tank in which locations?
options: On any nozzle that has an exterior protective coating
On the lowest shell course below the liquid level only
On the roof or within the vapor space, due to ignition risk
On the annular plate region near the shell-to-bottom weld
content.explanation: Hot taps are not permitted on the roof or in the vapor space, where flammable vapor and welding heat create an ignition hazard.

content.stem: A hot tap on a tank shell, where permitted, is controlled chiefly to manage:
options: The number of fixed-roof vents that are fitted on the tank roof structure
The exterior protective shell paint color match to the nearby storage tanks
The joint efficiency value that is used in the shell-design thickness formula
Burn-through and ignition given the remaining wall and contents
content.explanation: A permitted hot tap manages burn-through (wall thickness, heat input) and the flammability of the liquid and vapor in contact.

content.stem: Before reconstruction begins, API 653 requires the work to be authorized by:
options: An authorized inspector or an engineer experienced in tank design
The exterior protective coating contractor engaged for the storage tank
The operator alone, on the next routine in-service inspection round only
The supplier of the level gauge that is fitted to the fixed tank roof
content.explanation: Reconstruction must be authorized by an authorized API 653 inspector or a qualified tank engineer before work proceeds.

content.stem: In a reconstructed tank, the existing weld joints that are reused are:
options: Always cut out entirely and replaced regardless of their actual condition
Evaluated for acceptability, with new joints examined per the code
Exempt from any examination at all because they are not brand-new welds
Repainted on the exterior surface in place of any required examination
content.explanation: Reused existing joints are assessed for suitability while new/re-welded joints receive the required NDE before service.

content.stem: Materials used in tank reconstruction must:
options: Be selected only to minimize the material cost of the job
Match the exterior shell paint color of the original tank
Be exempt from any toughness consideration for the shell
Meet the applicable standard for the service and be documented
content.explanation: Reconstruction materials must conform to the applicable standard (and toughness needs) and be traceable/documented.

content.stem: After a reconstructed tank returns to service, API 653 expects the tank to be:
options: Exempt from any further inspection for twenty full years
Repainted a unique exterior color to flag the reconstruction
Marked with a nameplate recording the reconstruction details
Left unmarked to avoid confusing the operating personnel
content.explanation: A reconstructed (or significantly altered) tank gets a nameplate documenting the work, consistent with the marking/records requirements.

content.stem: The owner/operator records that API 653 expects to be maintained include:
options: Only the exterior protective shell paint purchase receipts for the tank
Construction, inspection, and repair/alteration records for the tank
Only the daily product temperature logs recorded for the stored fluid
Only the welder lunch and rest schedules during the original erection
content.explanation: Required records cover construction data, inspection history, and repair/alteration documentation, supporting future integrity decisions.

content.stem: The external and internal inspection reports for a tank must be prepared by:
options: The product scheduler in the operations department
The exterior coating subcontractor on the project
An authorized inspector responsible for the inspection
Any available employee regardless of qualification
content.explanation: Inspection reports are prepared/certified by the authorized inspector and become the official record of tank condition.

content.stem: API 653 inspection records for a tank are generally retained:
options: For the service life of the tank to support trending
Only until the next external inspection is performed
For exactly thirty days after each inspection visit
Only if the tank fails its next hydrostatic test event
content.explanation: Inspection and repair records are kept for the life of the tank so corrosion trends and prior decisions remain available.

content.stem: API 653 restricts lap-welded patch plates on a tank shell when the shell is:
options: Painted a darker exterior protective color than the adjacent storage tanks
Thicker than a defined limit (about 1/2 in.), where inserts are used instead
Storing a product with a specific gravity that is below one point zero
Fitted with more fixed-roof vents than the original design ever required
content.explanation: Lap patches are limited to thinner shells; above roughly 1/2 in. thickness, flush insert (butt) repairs are required.

content.stem: A flush insert (butt-welded) repair of a shell plate is preferred over a lap patch when:
options: A full-strength, flush joint is needed for the shell repair
The exterior shell paint color needs to be matched exactly
The tank's maximum fill height must be raised after repair
The cathodic protection potential needs to be increased now
content.explanation: Flush inserts restore the shell to a butt-welded, full-strength condition where a lap patch would be inadequate (e.g., thicker plate, higher stress).

content.stem: A door sheet cut into a tank shell for access must, on closure, be:
options: Re-welded and examined to restore the shell's integrity
Left bolted in place with an exterior gasket only
Painted over on the exterior without any re-welding
Replaced by a thinner plate to ease the welding work
content.explanation: A door-sheet opening is closed by re-welding the plate (often with specific joint details) and examined to confirm integrity before service.

content.stem: Adding or altering a shell penetration (nozzle) on an existing tank requires:
options: No engineering review because nozzles are minor items
Only an exterior coating around the new nozzle neck
Reinforcement and examination per the alteration requirements
A reduction of the tank's maximum fill height by default
content.explanation: New or altered penetrations are reinforced (area replacement) and examined as alterations under API 653/650.

content.stem: When a degraded tank condition exceeds the basic API 653 acceptance rules, the owner may apply:
options: A simple exterior repaint to restore the lost thickness
An API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 fitness-for-service assessment
An automatic twenty-year extension of the inspection
A reduction in the corrosion rate by administrative order
content.explanation: API 653 permits API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 fitness-for-service evaluation for conditions beyond the standard's basic screening rules.

content.stem: API 653 references which documents as the framework for risk-based inspection?
options: The product data sheet for the stored fluid only
Only the exterior paint specification for the tank
The cathodic protection criteria of RP 651 alone
API 580 and API 581 for the RBI methodology
content.explanation: RBI under API 653 follows API 580 (principles) and API 581 (methodology), combining likelihood and consequence of failure.

content.stem: A release prevention barrier (RPB) under a tank is provided to:
options: Increase the joint efficiency value of the lower shell course weld seams
Contain and help detect a bottom leak before it reaches the environment
Raise the brittle-fracture exemption temperature of the tank shell course
Serve as the exterior protective coating for the upper shell courses
content.explanation: An RPB (liner, double bottom, etc.) contains a bottom leak and aids detection, and it affects the allowable bottom minimum and intervals.

content.stem: Leak detection beneath a tank with a double bottom typically uses:
options: The cathodic protection rectifier repurposed as an underside flow meter
The exterior protective shell paint color used as a visual leak indicator
An interstitial monitoring space between the two bottoms
The product gauging float that is mounted on the fixed tank roof nozzle
content.explanation: A double bottom creates an interstitial space that is monitored (visually, vapor, or pressure) to detect a leak in the upper floor.

content.stem: Re-rating a tank to a higher liquid level or denser product requires:
options: Removal of the cathodic protection from the tank bottom
Only repainting the exterior shell to the new product color
No analysis because re-rating is purely an administrative step
An evaluation showing the shell and bottom satisfy the new loads
content.explanation: Re-rating to more severe service requires verifying the shell tmin, bottom, and toughness meet the new fill height/product loads.

content.stem: A tank storing concentrated sulfuric acid shows accelerated metal loss at a turbulent inlet where protective films are swept away. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Brittle fracture
Concentration cell corrosion
Atmospheric corrosion
Sulfuric acid corrosion
content.explanation: Velocity-accelerated loss in sulfuric acid, worst where turbulence strips the iron-sulfate film, is sulfuric acid corrosion.

content.stem: A tank bottom develops pitting beneath a gasketed connection where a stagnant crevice forms. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Concentration cell corrosion
Sulfuric acid corrosion
Brittle fracture
Atmospheric corrosion
content.explanation: A stagnant crevice under a gasket sets up differential concentration (a concentration cell), driving localized pitting.

content.stem: API 653 Annex B requires settlement measurement points spaced no more than 32 ft apart around the circumference, with at least 8 points. For a tank of diameter D = 150 ft, the minimum number of equally spaced points is:
options: 30 points
14 points
8 points
15 points
content.explanation: Circumference = pi x 150 = 471.2 ft; 471.2/32 = 14.7, rounded up to 15 (and at least 8), so 15 points are required.

content.stem: Using the same rule (<= 32 ft spacing, minimum 8 points), a small tank of diameter D = 60 ft requires a minimum number of measurement points of:
options: 8 points
6 points
12 points
16 points
content.explanation: Circumference = pi x 60 = 188.5 ft; 188.5/32 = 5.9, rounded up to 6, but the 8-point minimum governs, so 8 points are required.

content.stem: Tank D = 140 ft, H = 52 ft, G = 1.0, S = 24000 psi, E = 0.85. API 653 minimum shell thickness t = 2.6 D (H-1) G/(S E)?
A shell course has 0.45 in available for pressure design. With D = 90 ft, G = 1.0, S = 23200 psi, E = 0.85, the maximum fill height H = tSE/(2.6 D G) + 1 is:
Using MRT = min(RTbc, RTip) - Or(StPr + UPr): RTbc = 0.210 in, RTip = 0.250 in, Or = 12 yr, StPr = 0.003 in/yr, UPr = 0.004 in/yr. The MRT at the next inspection is:
External interval = lesser of 5 yr or RCA/(4N). Measured shell = 0.430 in, required = 0.360 in, N = 0.0045 in/yr. The external inspection interval is:
options: 3.9 years
7.8 years
5 years
15.6 years
content.explanation: RCA = 0.070. RCA/(4N) = 0.070/(4 x 0.0045) = 3.89; the lesser of 5 and 3.89 is 3.9 years.

content.stem: In API 653 Annex B, out-of-plane (differential) shell settlement is quantified as the:
options: Difference between the tank roof height and the nominal shell height
Absolute elevation read at the single lowest point on the shell
Average of all the shell-bottom elevations around the tank circumference
Deviation of the measured elevations from the best-fit cosine curve
content.explanation: Out-of-plane settlement is the deviation of measured points from the best-fit cosine curve that represents rigid-body tilt; that deviation is what stresses the shell.

content.stem: A best-fit cosine curve (Elev = a + b sin th + c cos th) is subtracted from the data because uniform and rigid (planar) tilt:
options: Do not by themselves induce stress in the tank shell
Always cause the shell to buckle at the lowest point
Are prohibited outright by the brittle-fracture rules
Increase the joint efficiency of the lower shell course
content.explanation: Uniform settlement and rigid tilt move the tank as a body without straining the shell; only the out-of-plane component (deviation from the cosine fit) matters structurally.

content.stem: When the measured settlement data does not fit a cosine curve acceptably, API 653 Annex B directs the evaluator to:
options: Declare the tank fit for continued service without any further analysis at all
Use the arc-based (B.3.2.2) procedure to find the permissible settlement
Average the high and the low readings together and ignore the curve fit entirely
Repaint the shell exterior surface and then re-measure the tank after thirty days
content.explanation: If the cosine fit is unacceptable, the arc method of B.3.2.2 is used to determine the maximum permissible out-of-plane settlement.

content.stem: The maximum permissible out-of-plane shell settlement determined by API 653 Annex B is capped at approximately:
options: 12 in. (about 304.8 mm), regardless of the computed value
1 in. (about 25.4 mm), regardless of the computed value
4 in. (about 101.6 mm), regardless of the computed value
No upper cap at all, since the formula governs entirely
content.explanation: Annex B caps the permissible out-of-plane settlement at about 4 in. even when the computation would otherwise allow more.

content.stem: API 653 Annex B evaluates edge settlement (near the shell-to-bottom joint) using:
options: Allowable-settlement curves (Bew and Be) selected by the local weld orientation
The same 2.6 D (H-1) G design formula that is used for shell-course thickness
Only the exterior protective shell paint condition observed at the settled location
The cathodic protection potential that is measured across the tank bottom plates
content.explanation: Edge settlement is judged against the Bew curve (lap welds ~parallel to the shell) or the less conservative Be curve (no welds, butt, or perpendicular lap), per the local weld orientation.

content.stem: For a tank under 200 ft in diameter, API 653 Annex B limits the settlement between two adjacent bottom points less than 10 ft apart to about:
options: 0.05 in. between the adjacent measurement points
5 in. between the adjacent measurement points
0.5 in. between the adjacent measurement points
No limit applies between adjacent bottom points
content.explanation: Localized bottom settlement between adjacent points spaced under 10 ft is limited to roughly 0.5 in. for tanks below about 200 ft diameter.

content.stem: The acceptability of the cosine-curve fit to the measured settlement data is judged by a:
options: Comparison of the shell paint color to a reference chart
Goodness-of-fit criterion (an R-squared value near 0.9)
Count of the nozzles installed in the lowest shell course
Measurement of the cathodic protection rectifier output
content.explanation: Annex B uses an R-squared goodness-of-fit criterion (around 0.9) to decide whether the cosine fit is acceptable before computing out-of-plane settlement.

content.stem: When measured settlement exceeds the Annex B acceptance limits, API 653 allows the owner to:
options: Perform an API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 assessment or relevel/repair the tank
Automatically extend the next inspection interval by a full twenty additional years
Ignore the exceedance entirely if the tank has never once leaked before this point
Raise the maximum allowable fill height to offset the differential settlement found
content.explanation: Exceeding Annex B limits triggers a fitness-for-service evaluation (API 579-1/ASME FFS-1), releveling, or repair, not continued operation as-is.

content.stem: API 653 Annex B specifies that shell settlement measurement points be spaced no more than:
options: One per shell course, regardless of the tank circumference size
100 ft apart around the circumference, with a minimum of 2 points
5 ft apart around the circumference, with a minimum of 50 points
32 ft apart around the circumference, with a minimum of 8 points
content.explanation: Annex B requires a maximum 32-ft spacing around the circumference and at least 8 measurement points to characterize settlement.

content.stem: API 650 requires butt-welded annular bottom plates (rather than lap-welded) when:
options: The roof is a cone roof rather than a dome roof structure on the storage tank itself
The tank is painted a darker exterior protective color than the nearby storage tanks
The product stress and thickness of the first shell course exceed set thresholds
Any nozzle whatsoever is added into the lowest course of the welded shell wall
content.explanation: Butt-welded annular plates are required when the first-course stress/thickness exceed API 650 thresholds, improving the shell-to-bottom junction under higher loads.

content.stem: An intermediate wind girder is added to an open-top tank to:
options: Increase the joint efficiency of the lower shell courses
Provide stability against shell buckling from wind pressure
Serve as the primary product-level gauge for the tank
Raise the brittle-fracture exemption temperature of the shell
content.explanation: Intermediate wind girders stiffen the upper shell of open-top tanks against wind-induced buckling.

content.stem: A frangible (weak) roof-to-shell joint on a fixed-roof tank is designed so that:
options: The tank becomes able to store a denser product than it was originally rated for
The roof can never separate from the shell under any operating condition whatsoever
The joint efficiency value of the shell automatically increases to one point zero
The roof-to-shell joint fails before the shell-to-bottom joint under overpressure
content.explanation: A frangible joint is the intended failure path under overpressure, venting at the roof-to-shell seam rather than rupturing the shell or bottom.

content.stem: The one-foot method for shell-thickness design in API 650 is limited to tanks with diameters:
options: Up to 200 ft; larger tanks use the variable-design-point method
Up to 50 ft; larger tanks use no thickness calculation at all
Of any size, with no restriction on the design method used
Only above 300 ft; smaller tanks use a fixed plate thickness
content.explanation: The one-foot method applies to tanks up to 200 ft diameter; above that the variable-design-point method is used.

content.stem: An API 653 brittle-fracture assessment of an existing tank chiefly considers the:
options: Material toughness, thickness, stress, and minimum metal temperature
The exterior protective shell paint color and the surface gloss level that is chosen
The number of fixed-roof vents that are fitted to the storage tank's fixed roof deck
The product gauging float type that is installed on the fixed tank roof deck plate
content.explanation: Brittle-fracture screening weighs toughness/material, thickness, stress level, and the lowest expected metal temperature against an exemption basis.

content.stem: An internal (out-of-service) inspection differs from a routine external inspection mainly because it:
options: Requires no qualified inspector since the tank is empty
Can be performed only from outside while the tank stays in service
Allows direct examination and thickness readings of the tank bottom
Is limited to checking the exterior shell paint condition
content.explanation: An internal inspection (tank emptied and cleaned) permits direct bottom examination and UT, which an external inspection cannot reach.

content.stem: A concrete ringwall foundation under a tank shell primarily serves to:
options: Act as the cathodic protection sacrificial anode for the entire tank bottom plate
Distribute the shell load and provide a stable, level bearing surface
Replace entirely the need for any bottom-plate corrosion allowance on the tank
Provide the product level indication reading for the aboveground storage tank
content.explanation: A ringwall spreads the concentrated shell load and gives a stable, well-drained, level base, reducing differential settlement at the shell.

content.stem: API RP 575 describes the use of which method for routine tank shell thickness monitoring?
options: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at established CMLs
Radiography of every square foot of the shell each year
Visual inspection of the exterior paint color only
Magnetic particle testing of the entire shell surface
content.explanation: RP 575 supports UT thickness monitoring at condition-monitoring locations to trend shell wall loss over time.

content.stem: Under API RP 651, a common criterion for adequate cathodic protection of a tank bottom is a:
options: Fixed rectifier current of exactly ten amperes at all times
Positive 850 mV potential relative to the surrounding soil mass
Negative 850 mV potential relative to a Cu/CuSO4 reference electrode
Shell paint thickness of at least ten mils on the exterior
content.explanation: RP 651 commonly cites the -850 mV (Cu/CuSO4) criterion (polarized or with IR considerations) for protected steel in soil.

content.stem: Before applying an internal lining to a tank bottom, API RP 652 emphasizes proper:
options: Reduction of the tank's maximum allowable fill height after the lining is applied
Selection of the exterior protective shell paint color used on the storage tank
Increase of the welded shell joint efficiency value up to one point zero exactly
Surface preparation, including abrasive blasting to the specified profile
content.explanation: RP 652 stresses surface preparation (cleanliness and anchor profile) as the foundation of a durable internal lining.

content.stem: Under API RP 577, the document that records the qualified ranges for a welding procedure is the:
options: Exterior shell paint specification for the storage tank
Procedure qualification record (PQR) supporting the WPS
Cathodic protection survey report for the tank bottom
Product gauging log kept by the operations department
content.explanation: RP 577 explains that the PQR documents the test results that qualify the WPS, including essential variable ranges.

content.stem: ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797), as referenced for API 653, addresses:
options: Radiographic film density limits and the penetrameter (IQI) selection rules
Ultrasonic thickness measurement by the manual contact pulse-echo method
Liquid penetrant dwell time and the developer application steps for the surface
Magnetic particle yoke lifting-force verification procedures for the technique
content.explanation: Article 23/SE-797 covers manual ultrasonic thickness measurement, the basis for shell/bottom UT readings.

content.stem: Under ASME Section IX, a change in an essential variable for a welding procedure requires:
options: An automatic increase in the shell joint efficiency
Only an exterior repaint of the affected shell area
No action because essential variables are advisory
Requalification of the welding procedure specification
content.explanation: A change to an essential variable affects mechanical properties and requires requalifying the WPS under Section IX.

content.stem: A buried portion of a tank bottom shows external metal loss correlated with soil resistivity and moisture, away from any stray current. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Brittle fracture
Caustic corrosion
Soil-side corrosion
Microbiologically influenced corrosion
content.explanation: External bottom loss driven by soil resistivity/moisture, absent a microbial signature or stray current, is soil-side corrosion.

content.stem: A tank bottom shows discrete hemispherical pits with tubercles and a rotten-egg odor in the deposits, under stagnant water-bottom conditions. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Concentrated sulfuric acid corrosion at the inlet
Soil-side external corrosion of the buried bottom
Atmospheric corrosion of the exposed surfaces
Microbiologically influenced corrosion
content.explanation: Tubercles, localized pitting, and sulfide odor under stagnant water point to microbiologically influenced corrosion (often SRB).
